disease_info: Bipolar I Disorder is characterized by at least one lifetime manic episode, typically lasting at least one week (or requiring hospitalization), often accompanied by marked impairment in social or occupational functioning. Manic episodes involve a distinct period of abnormally elevated or irritable mood and increased energy or activity, frequently associated with inflated self-esteem, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, impulsive behavior, and engagement in high-risk activities. Many patients also experience major depressive episodes over the course of illness, and the condition often follows a recurrent, episodic pattern with inter-episode recovery that can be incomplete. It is distinguished from Bipolar II Disorder by the presence of full mania rather than hypomania, and from primary psychotic disorders by the prominent mood component and episodic nature.

narrative.personality: Sheryl is socially magnetic, highly organized, and image-conscious, channeling her energy into meticulously planned social events and online content while privately managing anxiety through structured routines.
narrative.stressor: During her final semester of high school, Sheryl took on planning both prom and a large church youth conference while also trying to secure internships in event marketing, seeing these as make-or-break opportunities for her future. She began staying up later and later to perfect details, obsessing over budgets, layouts, and social media campaigns, telling herself that pushing harder would prove she was ready for a professional career. As the month went on, she kept adding new projects—volleyball fundraisers, volunteer drives at the animal shelter, and daily TikTok content—until nearly every waking hour was filled with self-imposed tasks, and she stopped attending classes regularly or following any kind of balanced routine. Her parents brought her to psychiatric care after teachers and church leaders reported that her behavior had become unmanageable, she was unable to follow through on basic school responsibilities, and she seemed driven by an unstoppable energy that was starting to damage her grades, relationships, and safety.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just can’t slow down—I’m constantly taking on more and more things and feel like I have to be doing something every minute.”

narrative.personality: Paulyn is a routine-oriented, community-minded planner who enjoys keeping things orderly while fostering fun, cooperative activities with friends and neighbors.
narrative.stressor: After leaving her barista job with the plan to "finally get serious" about finding an administrative assistant position, Paulyn suddenly had unstructured time and a strong desire to prove to herself and her family that she could build an adult life quickly. She began mapping out an ambitious schedule that included intensive job searching, organizing multiple community events, leading extra volunteer shifts, and starting new fitness and hobby projects all at once. Over the course of a month, what began as a focused transition plan escalated into a relentless drive to initiate new groups, committees, and social gatherings, crowding out sleep, basic self-care, and any downtime, and making it impossible for her to follow through consistently on job applications. Her parents encouraged her to seek psychiatric help when they noticed she was constantly launching new plans, talking about grand projects for the community while neglecting bills and household responsibilities, and becoming distressed when anyone suggested she slow down or prioritize.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve thrown myself into so many projects and plans lately that I can’t seem to stop starting new things, even though it’s getting in the way of actually getting a job.”

narrative.personality: Alyson is a conscientious, community-focused organizer who balances a love of structure and service with occasional spontaneous creative pursuits and quiet, reflective hobbies.
narrative.stressor: About six months after finalizing a difficult divorce and with her adult children living independently, Alyson found herself with more unstructured time and a strong desire to redefine her role in the community and in her family. When her daughter announced a surprise pregnancy and asked for help planning the baby shower, Alyson threw herself into the task, seeing it as a chance to be indispensable and to distract from lingering feelings of loneliness. Over the following month she increasingly volunteered for every available committee at the library and senior center, offered to mentor multiple younger volunteers, and started sketching out an ambitious series of historical workshops, often dominating conversations as she eagerly explained her ideas in great detail. Friends at her book club and a fellow library volunteer eventually suggested she see a psychiatrist when they noticed her talking nearly nonstop in meetings, signing up for more responsibilities than she could realistically manage, and becoming irritable when anyone questioned whether she was taking on too much.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I can’t seem to stop talking once I get going, and everyone keeps telling me I’m talking a mile a minute about all these projects I’ve taken on.”
